claims.claim: Explicit instruction is not a unitary intervention but a combination of more than a dozen teaching behaviours used to design and deliver instruction, which is why published definitions of it vary; the term also has to be separated from capital-letter 'Direct Instruction' programs.

Rosenshine's ten principles of instruction are a synthesis drawn from three separate bodies of work - cognitive science, observational studies of high-gain teachers, and research on cognitive supports - and their agreement is the argument for confidence in them; they are not the output of a single experiment.

Rosenshine reports an optimal success rate of roughly 80 percent during guided practice, and reports that more successful teachers spent more time in guided practice, questioning, checking for understanding and correcting errors, while less successful teachers gave shorter explanations and moved to worksheets; he also contrasts real checking with simply asking whether there are any questions.

Instructional guidance that benefits novices can become redundant and counterproductive as learner knowledge grows; the instructional implication drawn by the authors is that design must be tailored to the expertise of intended learners, and that without such tailoring the effectiveness of instructional designs is likely to be essentially arbitrary.

The IES practice guide Organizing Instruction and Study to Improve Student Learning recommends interleaving worked example solutions with problem-solving exercises at a moderate level of evidence, and rates asking deep explanatory questions and using quizzes to re-expose students to key content as strong, while rating other recommendations in the same guide low.

A federal practice guide rates a Model-Practice-Reflect instructional cycle at strong evidence for teaching writing strategies in grades 6-12, and a separate guide rates systematic instruction at strong evidence for elementary mathematics intervention.

Reviews of wait time report that when the average pause after a question exceeds roughly three seconds, teacher and student discourse changes and higher cognitive level achievement was obtained in elementary, middle and high school science, with achievement increases also reported in middle school mathematics; practitioner guidance likewise sets a three-second minimum of uninterrupted silence.

In a study of 16 sections of an undergraduate accounting course (5 high cold-calling sections with 196 students, 11 low cold-calling sections with 486 students), a significantly higher percentage of both men and women volunteered to answer questions in high cold-calling sections, women's volunteer question counts converged with men's in those sections, and increased cold-calling did not make either group uncomfortable.
'No Opt Out' is Technique #1 in Doug Lemov's Teach Like a Champion, a descriptive practitioner book of techniques drawn from classroom observation rather than an experimental research report.

A meta-analysis of classroom discussion found that several discussion approaches produced strong increases in student talk with reductions in teacher talk and substantial improvements in text comprehension, but that few approaches were effective at increasing students' literal or inferential comprehension and critical thinking and reasoning, with effects moderated by study design, outcome measure and student academic ability.

Cooperative learning as specified by Johnson and Johnson requires five structured elements - positive interdependence, individual and group accountability, promotive interaction, social skills, and group processing - and rests on social interdependence theory supported by more than 1,200 studies conducted over eleven decades.

Collaborative cognitive load theory predicts that for high-complexity tasks group members can learn more efficiently by distributing information across several working memories, while for low-complexity tasks the transaction costs of communicating and coordinating make individual learning more efficient.

Two meta-analyses across 164 studies found outcomes favourable to explicit instruction over unassisted discovery (580 comparisons, d = -0.38, 95% CI [-0.44, -0.31]) and favourable to enhanced or assisted discovery over other forms of instruction (360 comparisons, d = 0.30, 95% CI [0.23, 0.36]), with feedback, worked examples, scaffolding and elicited explanations identified as the helpful ingredients.

Defenders of problem-based and inquiry learning argue that those approaches were mistakenly conflated with unguided discovery and are in fact extensively scaffolded; this exchange is reported here rather than settled, and belongs to the constructivism lesson.

Interleaving is not uniformly effective: a meta-analysis of 59 studies, 158 samples and 238 effect sizes found an overall benefit of Hedges' g = 0.42 but strongly material-dependent results, including 0.67 for paintings, 0.34 for mathematics and -0.39 for words.

The ranked effect sizes in Hattie's Visible Learning are seriously criticised on statistical grounds, including common language effect values that fall outside the range of a probability, aggregation of incommensurable effects under single labels, and arbitrary baseline comparisons that determine the sign of an effect; a statistician's published critique calls the methodology pseudoscience.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether inquiry and problem-based learning are effective instructional strategies
positions: Kirschner, Sweller and Clark argue from human cognitive architecture that minimally guided instruction fails, and read inquiry and problem-based learning as instances of it
Hmelo-Silver, Duncan and Chinn reply that problem-based and inquiry learning are extensively scaffolded and were wrongly conflated with unguided discovery
Alfieri and colleagues' meta-analyses separate the two empirically: unassisted discovery loses to explicit instruction, enhanced or assisted discovery wins
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports the Alfieri separation as the practically useful resolution - the question is not inquiry versus explicit instruction but how much support the inquiry carries - and points readers to the constructivism lesson for the 2006-2007 exchange itself rather than relitigating it here.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How much weight to give ranked effect sizes for teaching strategies, particularly Hattie's Visible Learning
positions: Visible Learning presents a ranked barometer of influences on achievement drawn from over 800 meta-analyses
Bergeron's statistical critique identifies calculation errors, incommensurable aggregation and arbitrary baselines, and rejects the methodology
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson does not use Hattie's effect sizes as magnitudes. It names the critique specifically and contrasts the practice-guide model, in which each recommendation carries its own evidence rating for a stated population.

positions: A common instructor concern, cited in the cold-calling literature, is that cold calling makes students uncomfortable

Dallimore, Hertenstein and Platt report that high cold-calling sections had more voluntary participation from both men and women and that increased cold-calling did not make either group uncomfortable
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports the study's finding with its population stated (undergraduate accounting sections at one university) rather than generalising it to all classrooms, and separates it from the practitioner technique 'No Opt Out', which has no comparable evidence base.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive claims at all - only placeholder text asserting that instructional strategies is 'a foundational concept in Education' with a toolbox-drawer analogy and generic vocabulary entries. Nothing in it was verifiable or retained.
correctionsNeeded: Discarded the entire generated draft, including its vocabulary list, analogy, worked example and question bank.
Made strategy selection - not a catalogue of strategies - the spine of the lesson, on the strength of the expertise reversal literature.
Refused to cite Hattie effect sizes as settled magnitudes anywhere in the lesson, and taught the criticism of the method explicitly instead.
Separated explicit instruction from lecturing using the multicomponent definition rather than the common but unsupported equation of the two.
Attributed 'No Opt Out' to a descriptive practitioner book and said so, rather than presenting it as an evidence-based practice.
Reported the classroom-discussion meta-analysis with its negative finding included (few approaches raised critical thinking), rather than the usual one-sided summary.
rightsIssues: Most sources are peer-reviewed articles behind publisher terms or federal practice guides whose reuse terms were not separately verified; these are recorded REFERENCE_ONLY and no wording was reproduced from them.

Two sources are open access with explicit licences: the Dallimore et al. 2019 article states CC BY 4.0, and the Kirschner et al. 2018 article states CC BY 4.0. Both are still synthesised rather than quoted.
The Cooperative Learning Institute page is the Johnsons' own organisational site with no stated licence; recorded REFERENCE_ONLY and used only to confirm the five named elements.
The Lemov book is cited through its ERIC catalogue record for the technique name and publication type only; no content was reproduced.
Kalyuga et al. 2003 was read in full from a publicly hosted copy; the record points to the publisher's canonical page and the source is REFERENCE_ONLY.

sourceRecords.title: The Expertise Reversal Effect (Educational Psychologist, 38(1), 23-31)
sourceRecords.provider: Slava Kalyuga, Paul Ayres, Paul Chandler, John Sweller; Taylor & Francis
sourceRecords.notes: Full text read from a publicly hosted copy of the published article and text-extracted; the canonical publisher record is recorded here. Used for the definition of expertise reversal as a reversal in the relative effectiveness of instructional methods as learner knowledge changes, for its explanation as a form of the redundancy effect, for the imagination-versus-worked-example experiments in which the effect reversed with experience, and above all for the authors' instructional conclusion that design must be tailored to the expertise of intended learners and that without such tailoring the effectiveness of instructional designs is likely to be arbitrary. That conclusion is the spine of this lesson. No wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: How to Engage in Pseudoscience with Real Data: A Criticism of John Hattie's Arguments in 'Visible Learning' from the Perspective of a Statistician (McGill Journal of Education, 52(1))
sourceRecords.provider: Pierre-Jerome Bergeron, University of Ottawa; translated by Lysanne Rivard; McGill Journal of Education
sourceRecords.notes: Full text of the English translation downloaded from the journal and text-extracted, with the catalogue record confirmed through the ERIC API (EJ1150889). Used for the specific criticisms this lesson reports: that the common language effect values in Visible Learning can fall outside the range of a probability, a calculation error first flagged by Topphol in 2012; that Cohen's d cannot serve as a unit-free universal measure permitting comparison across arbitrarily different studies; that Hattie aggregates incommensurable effects under single labels; and that the choice of baseline comparison determines the sign of an effect, so a negative value need not mean a reverse effect. The article page states journal copyright with no Creative Commons licence, so it is reference only and no wording was reproduced.
